notes.meaning: The LORD speaks to Moses again. This chapter sets out the punishments for the sins already forbidden in chapters 18 and 19. Chapter 18 spoke to the person tempted to sin. This chapter speaks to the whole community, which had to enforce the law.

Molech was a false god, and his worship included giving children to him. Anyone living in Israel who did this, Israelite or foreigner, was to be stoned by the people. The whole community did the stoning because this was a sin against the whole nation. Abraham's offering of Isaac gives no excuse, because God called it off at once.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the wording could mean human sacrifice. It could also mean dedicating children to some kind of service of Molech. Some ancient versions read "to cause to serve."

notes.meaning: When God "sets His face against" someone, He treats that person as an enemy. Being "cut off" means being removed from God's people, and here God says He will do it Himself. These parents still came to worship God with this guilt on them. That "defiled" God's holy place, meaning it made it unclean. It also brought shame on God's name before others.

Neighbors or leaders might look the other way and let this crime go. If they did, God would act Himself. He would judge the man, his family, and everyone who followed him into this idol worship. "Prostituting themselves" is a picture of being unfaithful to God, like breaking a marriage.

Mediums and spiritists claimed to contact the dead or other spirits. Going to them for help was spiritual unfaithfulness. It gave the devil the honor that belongs to God alone. Here God Himself would punish the person who went to them. The mediums themselves are dealt with in verse 27.

In the middle of these hard laws comes a simple call: be holy. To "consecrate" yourself means to set yourself apart for God and keep clean from sin. Israel would show this by keeping God's laws. Yet it is the LORD who makes His people holy. His grace does not cancel our effort; it encourages it.

Cursing a parent here means bitter abuse or calling down evil on them, not just any angry word. It broke the command to honor father and mother, and it carried the death penalty. "His blood shall be upon him" means he is to blame for his own death. Jesus quoted this law in Matthew 15:4.

Adultery means sex with another person's husband or wife. Both the man and the woman were to be put to death. God treats it as a serious sin that wrongs the husband and breaks the marriage covenant. The penalty needed two or three eyewitnesses, so it was rarely carried out, but it set a clear line. One commentator explains that the moral rule still stands, but these death penalties belonged to Israel as a nation ruled by God.

Sex with a stepmother or a daughter-in-law was incest, meaning sexual sin with a close family member. Both people were to die. Chapter 18 forbade these acts, and here the penalty is given. "Acted perversely" means they turned upside down the order God set for families.

Sex between two men is called an abomination, something God finds deeply offensive. Both were to be put to death, the same penalty as for adultery and incest. Older commentators add that a person who was forced would not be guilty.

A man taking both a woman and her mother as wives was a terrible wickedness. Only those who agreed to it shared the guilt. The burning most likely came after death: the guilty were stoned, and then their bodies were burned.

A man or woman who had sex with an animal was to be put to death, and the animal was killed too. This showed how hateful the act was and wiped out any reminder of it. God condemns a lust that crosses a line even animals keep.
Sex with a sister or half-sister was a shameful act. They were to be "cut off in the sight of their people," a public punishment. "He shall bear his iniquity" means he carries his own guilt.

This verse forbids sex during a woman's monthly period, and both were to be cut off. The period itself was not a sin; it made a woman ritually unclean, which means unfit for worship for a time. God was teaching His people decency and self-control, even in marriage. Older commentators say this is about doing it on purpose, in contempt of the law.

Relations with an aunt, an uncle's wife, or a brother's wife were also forbidden. No death penalty from the court is named here; God kept the punishment for Himself. "They shall be childless" means God would deny them children, or their children would not count as rightful heirs. The one exception was a man marrying his dead brother's childless widow, which God allowed (Deuteronomy 25:5).

God calls Israel again to keep all His laws. Otherwise the land would "vomit them out," as it was doing to the nations living there. Those nations were being driven out because they did all these things, and God was disgusted by them. Belonging to God would not protect Israel if they sinned the same way.

God promised Israel a rich land "flowing with milk and honey," meaning full of good things. He had set them apart from all other peoples. This was so they would keep the knowledge and worship of the true God alive in the world.

Because God set Israel apart, Israel was to keep clean and unclean animals apart. Unclean animals were ones they must not eat, or touch when dead. These food laws were a daily reminder to stay away from the nations' impure ways. Christians read Acts 10 as showing that Christ's work has made clean what was once unclean.

Israel was to be holy because the LORD is holy. Here "holy" means set apart for God and growing to be like Him. He chose them out of the nations to be His very own treasure. He wanted a close relationship with them, not cold, mechanical obedience.

This law about mediums comes after the closing words, almost like an added note. Any man or woman who worked as a medium or spiritist was to be stoned. Those who went to them were cut off by God (verse 6). Those who practiced it were put to death by the people. This kept Israel from being stained by the worship of false gods.
